questions.stem: A 58 year old man has a 9 month history of attacks of spinning vertigo, each lasting 2 to 4 hours, with nausea. During attacks he hears a roaring noise in his left ear and his hearing on that side becomes muffled, partly recovering between attacks. Neurological examination between attacks is normal. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus is the classic triad of Ménière's disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: attacks of spinning vertigo, each lasting 2 to 4 hours
roaring noise in his left ear
hearing on that side becomes muffled
steps.x: Vertigo for minutes to hours, unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus together form the Ménière's triad.

elim: Causes slowly progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus, not discrete attacks of vertigo lasting hours.
Vertigo lasts seconds, is triggered by head position and has no hearing loss or tinnitus.
Usually headache or migraine features with attacks; fluctuating unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus point to the inner ear.
A single episode of vertigo lasting days, with no hearing loss or tinnitus.

steps.x: Answer C: Ménière's disease. Triad of episodic vertigo (minutes to hours), fluctuating unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus = Ménière's.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has had four attacks of rotatory vertigo over 3 months, each lasting about an hour, with ringing in her right ear and reduced hearing on that side. Her GP suspects Ménière's disease and asks about other symptoms during attacks. Otoscopy is normal. Her temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is most likely to be present during her attacks?
o: Feeling of pressure in the right ear
Weakness of the right side of the face
questions.e: Aural fullness, a sense of pressure in the affected ear, commonly accompanies the vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss of Ménière's.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional symptom is most likely to be present during her attacks?
The triad is already present; the fourth classic symptom of Ménière's is aural fullness in the same ear.

elim: Otorrhoea suggests otitis externa or chronic suppurative otitis media, not Ménière's.
Diplopia is a central (brainstem) feature and is a red flag against a peripheral cause.
Otalgia suggests infection; Ménière's is not painful.
Facial palsy suggests a cerebellopontine angle lesion or Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

steps.x: Answer C: Feeling of pressure in the right ear. Aural fullness (pressure in the ear) is the classic accompaniment of the Ménière's triad.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has recurrent attacks of vertigo with tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss in his left ear. Audiometry shows left low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and his GP diagnoses Ménière's disease. A medical student is asked to describe the timing that best separates this condition from other peripheral causes of vertigo.
questions.q: Which is the most likely duration of a single vertigo attack in this condition?
questions.e: Ménière's attacks last minutes to hours; BPPV lasts seconds and vestibular neuritis lasts days.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely duration of a single vertigo attack in this condition?

clues: fluctuating hearing loss in his left ear
steps.x: Use duration to sort peripheral vertigo: seconds = BPPV, minutes to hours = Ménière's, days = vestibular neuritis.

elim: Vertigo lasting seconds is typical of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Continuous vertigo for days is typical of vestibular neuritis.
Months of constant dizziness is not a pattern of any acute peripheral vestibular disorder.
Weeks of continuous vertigo is not typical of Ménière's; attacks are discrete and settle within hours.

steps.x: Answer B: Minutes to hours. BPPV seconds, Ménière's minutes to hours, vestibular neuritis days.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man has just been diagnosed with left-sided Ménière's disease after a year of episodic vertigo, tinnitus and muffled hearing. Audiometry shows a mild left sensorineural hearing loss. His attacks currently happen every few weeks. He asks what the condition is most likely to do to his ear over the next 10 to 20 years.
questions.q: Which is the most likely long-term complication?
o: Perforation of the left tympanic membrane
questions.e: Over time Ménière's tends to cause progressive, permanent sensorineural hearing loss in the affected ear.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely long-term complication?
Repeated hydrops damages cochlear hair cells, so the long-term complication is progressive hearing loss in that ear.

elim: Cholesteatoma is a middle ear complication of chronic otitis media, not of inner ear hydrops.
Ménière's affects the cochlea, so loss is sensorineural, not conductive.
The facial nerve is not damaged by endolymphatic hydrops.
The drum is unaffected; this follows infection or trauma.

steps.x: Answer E: Progressive left sensorineural hearing loss. Progressive sensorineural hearing loss is the long-term complication of Ménière's.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with known Ménière's disease is brought to the emergency department during an attack that began 2 hours ago. She is lying still, vomiting, with tinnitus and fullness in her left ear. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Vesicles in the left ear canal
questions.e: Ménière's attacks are debilitating, with nystagmus and balance problems; central signs such as dysarthria or past-pointing are absent.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: during an attack that began 2 hours ago
steps.x: During an acute peripheral vestibular attack you expect nystagmus and poor balance, without cerebellar or cranial nerve signs.

elim: Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure, not an inner ear disorder.
These are cerebellar signs and suggest a central cause such as posterior circulation stroke.
Facial weakness points to a cerebellopontine angle lesion or Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
Vesicles suggest Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus).

steps.x: Answer D: Nystagmus with unsteadiness on standing. A Ménière's attack gives nystagmus and imbalance; central signs suggest another diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has had attacks of vertigo for a year, lasting 1 to 3 hours, with buzzing tinnitus and muffled hearing in her right ear. Between attacks she feels well. Cranial nerve examination is normal. Audiometry shows right low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent hour-long vertigo, unilateral low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus with normal examination between attacks is Ménière's disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: attacks of vertigo for a year, lasting 1 to 3 hours
muffled hearing in her right ear
steps.x: Recurrent attacks plus unilateral sensorineural loss means an inner ear disorder involving both cochlea and vestibule.

elim: Labyrinthitis is a single prolonged episode of vertigo with hearing loss, usually after a viral illness, not recurrent attacks.
Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss without attacks of vertigo.
Stroke causes sudden persistent vertigo with central signs and does not recur in hour-long attacks with normal examination.
Age-related hearing loss is bilateral, high-frequency and has no vertigo.

steps.x: Answer B: Ménière's disease. Recurrent vertigo + unilateral SNHL + tinnitus = Ménière's, which affects both cochlea and vestibular system.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has a 6 month history of episodes of vertigo lasting about 2 hours, accompanied by tinnitus and a muffled feeling in his right ear. Audiometry shows right sensorineural hearing loss and MRI of the brain and internal auditory meatus is normal. A student asks where the problem is.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?
o: Cochlea and vestibular apparatus of the inner ear
questions.e: Ménière's affects the whole inner ear, so the cochlea (hearing, tinnitus) and the vestibular system (vertigo) are both involved.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely site of the lesion?

clues: tinnitus and a muffled feeling in his right ear
MRI of the brain and internal auditory meatus is normal
steps.x: Vertigo plus sensorineural hearing loss with normal imaging means both inner ear organs are involved.

elim: A cerebellopontine angle lesion (acoustic neuroma) would show on MRI, which is normal.
Ossicle disease causes conductive hearing loss without vertigo.
Drum disease causes conductive hearing loss, not vertigo with sensorineural loss.
Isolated vestibular nerve inflammation (vestibular neuritis) spares hearing.

steps.x: Answer B: Cochlea and vestibular apparatus of the inner ear. Ménière's is an inner ear disorder affecting both cochlea and vestibular system.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman is seen during an attack of rotatory vertigo with tinnitus and fullness in her left ear, similar to previous attacks lasting hours. She has horizontal nystagmus. When her head is turned rapidly to the left while she fixes on the examiner's nose, her eyes are dragged with the head and then flick back to the target.
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of the head impulse test?
questions.e: A corrective saccade on the head impulse test indicates a peripheral vestibular lesion, as in Ménière's disease.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely interpretation of the head impulse test?

clues: eyes are dragged with the head and then flick back to the target
tinnitus and fullness in her left ear
steps.x: The flick back is a corrective saccade, meaning the vestibulo-ocular reflex on that side has failed: a peripheral lesion.

elim: A central lesion usually gives a normal head impulse test, so an abnormal test points away from stroke.
Cerebellar lesions give central signs and a normal head impulse test.
A corrective saccade is an objective sign and cannot be produced voluntarily.
In a normal test the eyes stay on target with no corrective saccade.

steps.x: Answer E: Peripheral vestibular lesion. Corrective saccade on head impulse test = peripheral lesion.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man attends the emergency department with 3 hours of severe spinning vertigo and vomiting. He has had five similar attacks over a year, each with ringing and dulled hearing in his right ear, settling within a day. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 134/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Gait is unsteady but there are no cerebellar signs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent attacks lasting hours with unilateral tinnitus and hearing loss are Ménière's; the absence of cerebellar signs argues against stroke.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: five similar attacks over a year
ringing and dulled hearing in his right ear
steps.x: Recurrent, hours-long attacks with cochlear symptoms in one ear, and no central signs.

elim: BPPV lasts seconds with head movement and causes no hearing loss.
Labyrinthitis is a single episode lasting days, not recurrent attacks.
Repeated identical attacks that resolve, with no cerebellar signs, make stroke unlikely.
Vestibular neuritis does not affect hearing and lasts days.

steps.x: Answer C: Ménière's disease. Recurrent hours-long vertigo with unilateral cochlear symptoms = Ménière's.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting 1 to 2 hours, with tinnitus, aural fullness and fluctuating hearing in her left ear. Audiometry shows left low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. MRI of the internal auditory meatus is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her symptoms?
o: Benign tumour of the vestibular nerve
Calcium debris in the posterior semicircular canal
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
questions.e: Ménière's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops, an excess of endolymph raising pressure in the inner ear.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her symptoms?

clues: recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting 1 to 2 hours
fluctuating hearing in her left ear
MRI of the internal auditory meatus is normal
steps.x: The triad with normal imaging is Ménière's; its cause is excess endolymph pressure.

elim: A vestibular schwannoma would be seen on MRI, which is normal.
Canal debris causes BPPV, with seconds of positional vertigo and normal hearing.
This is otosclerosis, which causes conductive loss without vertigo.
This is vestibular neuritis, a single days-long episode without hearing loss.

steps.x: Answer C: Endolymphatic hydrops. Ménière's = endolymphatic hydrops.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman was told a year ago that she had vestibular neuritis. Since then she has had six further attacks of vertigo, each lasting 2 to 3 hours rather than days, with tinnitus and muffled hearing in her right ear. Between attacks she is well. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent attacks lasting hours with cochlear symptoms fit Ménière's; vestibular neuritis lasts days and spares hearing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: each lasting 2 to 3 hours rather than days
tinnitus and muffled hearing in her right ear
steps.x: The duration (hours, not days) and the hearing symptoms rule out vestibular neuritis.

elim: An acoustic neuroma causes gradual hearing loss, not recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting hours.
BPPV attacks last seconds and do not cause tinnitus or hearing loss.
Vestibular neuritis lasts days and spares hearing.
No headache or migraine features are given, and fluctuating unilateral hearing loss points to the inner ear.

steps.x: Answer C: Ménière's disease. Hours with hearing loss = Ménière's; days without hearing loss = vestibular neuritis.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has recurrent hour-long attacks of vertigo with roaring tinnitus and muffled hearing in his left ear. His GP arranges a hearing test before referral. Otoscopy is normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on audiometry?
questions.e: Audiometry in Ménière's typically shows unilateral sensorineural hearing loss on the affected side, often low frequency.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on audiometry?

clues: muffled hearing in his left ear
steps.x: Inner ear disease on the left gives left sensorineural loss; a normal drum makes conductive loss unlikely.

elim: This is presbycusis, which is symmetrical and age-related.
Ménière's is a cochlear disorder, so hearing loss is sensorineural, not conductive.
Ménière's typically shows unilateral sensorineural loss on audiometry.
His symptoms are in the left ear, so the loss is on the left.

steps.x: Answer C: Left sensorineural hearing loss. Audiometry in Ménière's: sensorineural loss in the affected ear.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has a 7 month history of attacks of vertigo lasting 1 to 4 hours, with right-sided tinnitus, aural fullness and fluctuating hearing. Neurological examination is normal and audiometry shows right sensorineural hearing loss. She asks which single test will prove she has Ménière's disease.
questions.q: How is the diagnosis of Ménière's disease confirmed?
o: Clinical diagnosis from the history and examination
questions.e: Ménière's is a clinical diagnosis: typical attacks plus audiometric sensorineural loss, with other causes excluded.

steps.x: The question asks: How is the diagnosis of Ménière's disease confirmed?

clues: attacks of vertigo lasting 1 to 4 hours
audiometry shows right sensorineural hearing loss
steps.x: There is no single confirmatory test; the diagnosis rests on the clinical picture supported by audiometry.

elim: No scan proves Ménière's; CT has no role in confirming it.
This diagnoses BPPV, not Ménière's.
CSF analysis has no role in inner ear disease.
Blood tests do not diagnose Ménière's.

steps.x: Answer A: Clinical diagnosis from the history and examination. Ménière's is a clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has episodic vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss in his right ear. Audiometry shows an asymmetric right sensorineural hearing loss. His ENT surgeon requests MRI of the brain with internal auditory meatus views before confirming Ménière's disease.
questions.q: Which condition is this scan mainly intended to exclude?
questions.e: MRI is used second-line to exclude other causes of asymmetric sensorineural loss, especially an acoustic neuroma at the cerebellopontine angle.

steps.x: The question asks: Which condition is this scan mainly intended to exclude?
Asymmetric sensorineural loss must have a tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve excluded.

elim: BPPV is diagnosed clinically with the Dix-Hallpike test; MRI is normal.
This is seen on otoscopy and tympanometry and causes conductive loss.
Otosclerosis causes conductive loss and is not the reason for MRI here.
Vestibular neuritis is clinical and MRI does not exclude it.

steps.x: Answer E: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma). MRI in suspected Ménière's excludes an acoustic neuroma.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting hours with left tinnitus. Audiometry shows a left sensorineural hearing loss that is clearly worse than the right. Neurological examination is normal. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: MRI brain with internal auditory meatus views
questions.e: After audiometry shows asymmetric sensorineural loss, MRI brain is the second-line test to exclude an acoustic neuroma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

clues: Audiometry shows a left sensorineural hearing loss
steps.x: First-line audiometry is done; the next step for asymmetric loss is MRI.

elim: Caloric testing does not exclude a structural cause of asymmetric hearing loss.
The sinuses are irrelevant to vertigo and sensorineural loss.
EEG is for seizures, not vertigo with hearing loss.
Asymmetric sensorineural loss needs a structural cause excluded now, not delayed.

steps.x: Answer D: MRI brain with internal auditory meatus views. Audiometry first, then MRI to exclude other causes.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has had three attacks of vertigo in 2 months, each lasting about 90 minutes, with tinnitus and dulled hearing in his right ear. Between attacks he is well and neurological examination is normal. Rinne's and Weber's tests are difficult to interpret. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Audiometry is the first-line investigation in suspected Ménière's and typically shows sensorineural hearing loss.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

clues: dulled hearing in his right ear
steps.x: Hearing symptoms need objective measurement; bedside tests are unclear, so arrange formal audiometry.

elim: There is no fever or sign of infection.
CT is not used for suspected Ménière's and does not assess hearing.
This tests for BPPV, whose attacks last seconds without hearing loss.
Vertigo with cochlear symptoms is not a cardiac presentation.

steps.x: Answer A: Audiometry. First-line test for suspected Ménière's = audiometry.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with Ménière's disease has a severe attack of vertigo with nausea and right-sided tinnitus. Her GP prescribes prochlorperazine to relieve the acute symptoms. She asks how long she should take it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of treatment?
o: A short course of 1 to 2 weeks
Until her hearing returns to normal
questions.e: Prochlorperazine is for acute symptom relief only, given as a short course of 1 to 2 weeks.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate duration of treatment?
Acute vestibular suppressants are short term; long courses cause side effects.

elim: A single dose is usually not enough to control an attack that lasts hours to days of after-effects.
Prochlorperazine is not a preventer; long-term use risks extrapyramidal side effects. Betahistine is used for prevention.
Prolonged vestibular suppressant use delays compensation and causes side effects.
Hearing may never fully recover; this is not a treatment end point.

steps.x: Answer A: A short course of 1 to 2 weeks. Prochlorperazine: short course, 1 to 2 weeks.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has been diagnosed with Ménière's disease. He has an attack every 2 to 3 months. He drinks six cups of coffee a day, eats a lot of processed food and drinks 25 units of alcohol a week. His BP is 128/80 mmHg. He would like to reduce his attacks without starting a drug.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: High fluid and high salt intake
Low salt diet and cut down caffeine and alcohol
questions.e: Lifestyle measures are first line: a low salt diet and avoiding caffeine and alcohol.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: six cups of coffee a day
steps.x: His triggers are salt, caffeine and alcohol; first-line advice targets these.

elim: Flying is not a recognised trigger to avoid in Ménière's.
The Epley manoeuvre treats BPPV.
Salt worsens fluid retention and may worsen hydrops; a low salt diet is advised.
Rehabilitation helps chronic imbalance but does not address his triggers.

steps.x: Answer D: Low salt diet and cut down caffeine and alcohol. First-line Ménière's lifestyle: low salt, avoid caffeine and alcohol.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has had Ménière's disease for 18 months. She follows a low salt diet and avoids caffeine but now has two or three attacks a month, each needing time off work. Her last attack settled a week ago and she currently has no vertigo. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to reduce the frequency of her attacks?
questions.e: Betahistine is used to prevent recurrent attacks once acute symptoms have settled.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug to reduce the frequency of her attacks?

clues: two or three attacks a month
steps.x: Lifestyle has failed and she is between attacks, so start a preventer.

elim: Amitriptyline is used for neuropathic pain or migraine prophylaxis, not Ménière's prevention.
Steroids are not first choice for preventing Ménière's attacks.
Prochlorperazine is for short courses in acute attacks only.
Sumatriptan treats migraine attacks.

steps.x: Answer B: Betahistine. Betahistine prevents recurrent Ménière's attacks.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has disabling right-sided Ménière's disease. Over 2 years he has followed a low salt diet, avoided caffeine and alcohol and taken betahistine, yet he still has weekly attacks that stop him working. Audiometry shows worsening right sensorineural loss. MRI is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase the betahistine and review in 2 years
questions.e: Severe Ménière's refractory to lifestyle and betahistine is treated with intratympanic injections, or rarely surgery.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
First-line and second-line treatment have failed: this is refractory disease.

elim: Implants are for profound hearing loss and do not control vertigo attacks.
This repositions canal debris in BPPV.
His disease is already refractory to betahistine; delaying is inappropriate.
Prochlorperazine is for short acute courses only.

steps.x: Answer B: ENT referral for intratympanic injection. Refractory Ménière's: intratympanic injections, rarely surgery.

questions.stem: A 43 year old woman with Ménière's disease has had 4 hours of severe vertigo and vomiting with left tinnitus. This is her fourth attack this month. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. She asks for treatment now and something to prevent further attacks.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management plan?
o: Betahistine now and stop when the vertigo settles
Epley manoeuvre now, then vestibular rehabilitation
Prochlorperazine now, then betahistine once the attack settles
questions.e: Acute attacks are treated with a short course of prochlorperazine; betahistine is started once acute symptoms settle to prevent recurrence.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management plan?

clues: 4 hours of severe vertigo and vomiting
steps.x: Two needs: acute symptom relief now and prevention later.

elim: Betahistine is a preventer started after the acute attack, not an acute treatment that is stopped.
The Epley manoeuvre is for BPPV.
Intratympanic treatment is reserved for refractory disease, not first presentation of frequent attacks.
Prochlorperazine is a short 1 to 2 week course.

steps.x: Answer E: Prochlorperazine now, then betahistine once the attack settles. Acute = prochlorperazine; prevention after settling = betahistine.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has newly diagnosed left Ménière's disease. He has had two mild attacks in 6 months, each settling within an hour. His hearing is normal between attacks. He is keen to avoid medication if possible. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Lifestyle advice: low salt diet and avoid caffeine and alcohol
Surgical decompression of the endolymphatic sac
questions.e: First-line management of Ménière's is lifestyle change: low salt diet and avoiding caffeine and alcohol.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Infrequent, mild disease and a wish to avoid drugs: start with lifestyle.

elim: With infrequent mild attacks, lifestyle measures come first; betahistine is added if attacks recur often.
Reserved for severe refractory disease.
Prochlorperazine is a short course for acute attacks, not continuous treatment.
Surgery is rare and only for refractory disease.

steps.x: Answer C: Lifestyle advice: low salt diet and avoid caffeine and alcohol. Start Ménière's management with lifestyle measures.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with known Ménière's disease visits her GP 3 hours into an attack of rotatory vertigo with nausea, right-sided tinnitus and aural fullness. Examination shows horizontal nystagmus and no focal neurological signs. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Following NICE CKS guidance, the GP prescribes a drug for acute symptom relief.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug?
questions.e: NICE CKS: a short course of prochlorperazine relieves an acute Ménière's attack; betahistine is for prevention.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug?
Acute attack, no central signs: use the vestibular suppressant.

elim: There is no infection.
Betahistine prevents recurrent attacks; it is not the acute treatment.
Benzodiazepines are not the standard acute treatment and cause sedation and dependence.
An NSAID does not suppress vertigo.

steps.x: Answer E: Prochlorperazine. Acute Ménière's attack = prochlorperazine.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with Ménière's disease is given prochlorperazine for an acute attack of vertigo and vomiting. His symptoms improve within a day. A pharmacology student asks how the drug works.
questions.q: Which is the main mechanism of action of prochlorperazine?
questions.e: Prochlorperazine is a dopamine D2 antagonist with antihistaminergic and anticholinergic vestibular suppressant activity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main mechanism of action of prochlorperazine?

clues: acute attack of vertigo and vomiting
steps.x: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine: blocks dopamine D2 receptors, with extra antihistamine and anticholinergic effects.

elim: This is ondansetron.
This is the mechanism of benzodiazepines.
This is part of betahistine's action.
Prochlorperazine has antimuscarinic, not muscarinic agonist, activity.

steps.x: Answer B: Dopamine D2 receptor antagonist. Prochlorperazine = D2 antagonist (plus antihistamine and anticholinergic).

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with Ménière's disease starts betahistine to reduce the frequency of her attacks. Her attacks become less frequent over the next 3 months. She asks how the tablet works.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of betahistine?
o: Weak histamine H1 agonist and H3 antagonist
questions.e: Betahistine is a histamine analogue: weak H1 agonist and H3 antagonist, thought to increase cochlear blood flow and modulate vestibular nerve activity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of betahistine?

clues: reduce the frequency of her attacks
steps.x: Betahistine is a histamine analogue, so it acts on histamine receptors as an agonist at H1.

elim: This is acetazolamide.
This is prochlorperazine, used for acute attacks.
Betahistine is an H1 agonist, not an antagonist.
This is furosemide.

steps.x: Answer E: Weak histamine H1 agonist and H3 antagonist. Betahistine = weak H1 agonist / H3 antagonist, raising cochlear blood flow.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has recurrent attacks of vertigo with fluctuating left-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. He has been diagnosed with endolymphatic hydrops. He asks why one problem in the inner ear causes all three symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Compression of the vestibulocochlear nerve by a tumour
Distension of the endolymphatic system distorting cochlear and vestibular hair cells
Free otoconia moving within a semicircular canal
Ischaemia of the brainstem vestibular nuclei
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve
questions.e: In Ménière's the distended endolymphatic system distorts the hair cells of both the cochlea (hearing loss, tinnitus) and vestibular organs (vertigo).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
Hydrops affects the whole membranous labyrinth, so both sets of hair cells are distorted.

elim: This is an acoustic neuroma.
This is BPPV.
This is a central (stroke) cause.
This is vestibular neuritis, which spares hearing.

steps.x: Answer B: Distension of the endolymphatic system distorting cochlear and vestibular hair cells. Distended endolymph distorts cochlear and vestibular hair cells.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has Ménière's disease affecting her right ear. Her ENT surgeon explains that the excess inner ear fluid probably results from a problem with how the fluid is removed rather than how it is made.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the excess fluid?
o: Impaired endolymph resorption at the endolymphatic sac
Leak of perilymph through the round window
questions.e: The exact cause is unclear, but Ménière's may relate to impaired endolymph resorption at the endolymphatic sac.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of the excess fluid?

clues: problem with how the fluid is removed
steps.x: Endolymph is resorbed at the endolymphatic sac; poor resorption leads to hydrops.

elim: CSF drainage problems cause hydrocephalus, not inner ear hydrops.
This causes middle ear effusion and conductive loss.
A perilymph fistula is a different disorder.
